claims.source: For example, NEUROD1 is required for photoreceptor survival, and BHLHE22 and BHLHE23 are required for development of OFF cone bipolar cells and rod bipolar cells, respectively (Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003.

claims.claim: BHLHE22 is required for development of OFF cone bipolar cells.
claims.source: For example, NEUROD1 is required for photoreceptor survival, and BHLHE22 and BHLHE23 are required for development of OFF cone bipolar cells and rod bipolar cells, respectively (Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003.

claims.claim: BHLHE23 is required for development of rod bipolar cells.
claims.source: For example, NEUROD1 is required for photoreceptor survival, and BHLHE22 and BHLHE23 are required for development of OFF cone bipolar cells and rod bipolar cells, respectively (Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bramblett et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2014; Pennesi et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The cis-regulatory elements of mouse rods and cones are strongly enriched for K50 HD motifs.
claims.source: Our lab has previously shown that the cis-regulatory elements (CREs; i.e., enhancers and promoters) of mouse rods and cones are strongly enriched for K50 HD motifs as well as moderately enriched for Q50 HD and E-box motifs (Hughes et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2017.

claims.claim: K50 HD motifs are positively correlated with enhancer activity in photoreceptors.
claims.source: In addition, we recently used a massively parallel reporter assay to analyze the activity of thousands of photoreceptor enhancers identified by CRX ChIP-seq and found that both K50 HD and E-box motifs are positively correlated with enhancer activity in photoreceptors while Q50 HD motifs have a weakly negative correlation with enhancer activity (Hughes et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2018.

claims.claim: E-box motifs are positively correlated with enhancer activity in photoreceptors.
claims.source: In addition, we recently used a massively parallel reporter assay to analyze the activity of thousands of photoreceptor enhancers identified by CRX ChIP-seq and found that both K50 HD and E-box motifs are positively correlated with enhancer activity in photoreceptors while Q50 HD motifs have a weakly negative correlation with enhancer activity (Hughes et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Q50 HD motifs have a weakly negative correlation with enhancer activity in photoreceptors.
claims.source: In addition, we recently used a massively parallel reporter assay to analyze the activity of thousands of photoreceptor enhancers identified by CRX ChIP-seq and found that both K50 HD and E-box motifs are positively correlated with enhancer activity in photoreceptors while Q50 HD motifs have a weakly negative correlation with enhancer activity (Hughes et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Q50 HD motifs mediate weak activation of expression via RAX.
claims.source: In contrast, studies of individual reporters have shown that Q50 HD motifs mediate weak activation of expression via RAX, and that RAX can either enhance or suppress the transactivation activity of CRX, depending upon RAX expression levels (Irie et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Irie et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2000.

claims.claim: RAX can either enhance or suppress the transactivation activity of CRX, depending upon RAX expression levels.
claims.source: In contrast, studies of individual reporters have shown that Q50 HD motifs mediate weak activation of expression via RAX, and that RAX can either enhance or suppress the transactivation activity of CRX, depending upon RAX expression levels (Irie et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Irie et al., 2015; Kimura et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Q50 motifs in bipolar cells appear to be strongly repressive when bound by VSX2.
claims.source: In contrast, Q50 motifs in bipolar cells appear to be strongly repressive when bound by VSX2, which has been proposed to inhibit the expression of photoreceptor genes in bipolar cells (Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Dorval et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Dorval et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2008.

claims.claim: VSX2 has been proposed to inhibit the expression of photoreceptor genes in bipolar cells.
claims.source: In contrast, Q50 motifs in bipolar cells appear to be strongly repressive when bound by VSX2, which has been proposed to inhibit the expression of photoreceptor genes in bipolar cells (Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Dorval et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Dorval et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Single base pair substitutions that interconvert Q50 and K50 half-sites within dimeric motifs are sufficient to switch the specificity of opsin expression within photoreceptor sub-types in Drosophila.
claims.source: Indeed, a recent study in Drosophila showed that single base pair substitutions that interconvert Q50 and K50 half-sites within dimeric motifs are sufficient to switch the specificity of opsin expression within photoreceptor sub-types (Rister et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rister et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Adult Otx2-GFP mice display high-level GFP in bipolar cells and low-level expression in photoreceptors.
claims.source: Adult Otx2-GFP mice display high-level GFP in bipolar cells and low-level expression in photoreceptors (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing fluorescence patterns.

claims.claim: In Grm6-YFP mice, YFP is driven by the Grm6 promoter and expressed only in ON bipolar cells.
claims.source: To purify ON and OFF bipolar cells separately, we crossed Otx2-GFP mice with a Grm6-YFP line, in which YFP is driven by the Grm6 promoter and expressed only in ON bipolar cells (Morgan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Morgan et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Purity of bipolar cell populations was confirmed by RT-qPCR which showed enrichment of ON- and OFF-specific genes in the appropriate populations.
claims.source: Purity of bipolar cell populations was confirmed by RT-qPCR which showed enrichment of ON- and OFF-specific genes in the appropriate populations and depletion of markers for other retinal cell classes as compared to whole retina (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: RNA-seq generated highly reproducible profiles across biological replicates for bipolar cells.
claims.source: We then used RNA-seq to profile gene expression in purified populations of bipolar cells, obtaining highly reproducible profiles across biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Mouse photoreceptors lacking Nrl transdifferentiate into blue cones during development.
claims.source: We used Nrl-/- photoreceptors as a surrogate for blue cones (i.e., Opn1sw-expressing cones) since mouse photoreceptors lacking Nrl transdifferentiate into blue cones during development (Daniele et al., 2005; Nikonov et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Daniele et al., 2005; Nikonov et al., 2005.

claims.claim: 5259 genes have at least a two-fold difference in expression between bipolar cells and either rods or blue cones (FDR < 0.05).
claims.source: We identified a total of 5259 genes with at least a two-fold difference in expression between bipolar cells and either rods or blue cones (FDR < 0.05) (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The bipolar cell transcriptome is more similar to that of photoreceptors than to that of any other retinal cell class.
claims.source: Despite the large number of differentially expressed genes, published single-cell RNA-seq profiles indicate that the bipolar cell transcriptome is more similar to that of photoreceptors than to that of any other retinal cell class (Macosko et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Macosko et al., 2015.

claims.claim: 394 of the differentially expressed genes between photoreceptors and bipolar cells encode putative transcriptional regulators.
claims.source: Next, we compared the list of differentially expressed genes to a database of mouse TFs (AnimalTFDB3.0; Hu et al., 2019), which revealed that 394 of the differentially expressed genes encode putative transcriptional regulators (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to the AnimalTFDB3.0 database (Hu et al., 2019).

claims.claim: 680 genes were differentially expressed by at least two-fold between ON and OFF bipolar cells (FDR < 0.05).
claims.source: In contrast, comparison of the transcriptomes of ON and OFF bipolar cells identified only 680 genes that were differentially expressed by at least two-fold (317 ON- and 363 OFF-enriched at FDR < 0.05; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The number of differentially expressed genes between ON and OFF bipolar cells is less than half of the number between rods and blue cones.
claims.source: This figure is less than half of the number of differentially expressed genes identified between rods and blue cones (1,471), indicating that the transcriptomes of the two categories of bipolar cells are quite similar.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Expression estimates from bulk and pooled pseudo-bulk single-cell RNA-seq are well correlated (Pearson correlation coefficients range from 0.82 to 0.85).
claims.source: We found that expression estimates from bulk and pooled pseudo-bulk single-cell RNA-seq are well correlated (Pearson correlation coefficients range from 0.82 to 0.85, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: 50 of the 680 differentially expressed genes found in bulk analysis were not present in the Drop-seq data.
claims.source: Additionally, 50 of the 680 differentially expressed genes found in our bulk analysis were not present in the Drop-seq data (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of bulk RNA-seq data with Drop-seq data.

claims.claim: ATAC-seq generated highly reproducible profiles across biological replicates for bipolar cells (Pearson correlation 0.95–1.00).
claims.source: Similar to our RNA-seq data, ATAC-seq generated highly reproducible profiles across biological replicates (Pearson correlation 0.95–1.00, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: More than 345,000 open chromatin regions were identified by combining ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data.
claims.source: To compare chromatin accessibility across tissues, we combined ATAC-seq peaks from bipolar cells with previously generated ATAC-seq data from purified mouse rods, blue cones, and 'green' cones (i.e., Opn1mw-expressing cones) as well as DNase-seq data from whole retina, brain, heart, and liver to obtain a list of > 345,000 open chromatin regions (Hughes et al., 2017; ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by combining ATAC-seq and DNase-seq datasets.

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering of chromatin accessibility profiles at enhancers showed that photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and whole retina cluster separately from other tissues.
claims.source: Hierarchical clustering of chromatin accessibility profiles at enhancers showed that photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and whole retina cluster separately from other tissues (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Whole retina DNase-seq clustered with bipolar cell samples.
claims.source: We found that whole retina DNase-seq clustered with bipolar cell samples (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: More than half of the whole retina peaks did not overlap with photoreceptor peaks.
claims.source: This is in line with our previous comparison of genome-wide patterns of chromatin accessibility in rods, cones and whole retina, which showed that more than half of the whole retina peaks did not overlap with photoreceptor peaks, suggesting that they derive from non-photoreceptor retinal cell types (Hughes et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2017.

claims.claim: 55,402 differentially accessible regions were identified between photoreceptor and bipolar cells (FDR < 0.05).
claims.source: Finally, direct comparison of ATAC-seq peaks from photoreceptor and bipolar cells identified 55,402 differentially accessible regions (FDR < 0.05), 75% of which are more accessible in bipolar cells (Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 75% of differentially accessible regions between photoreceptors and bipolar cells are more accessible in bipolar cells.
claims.source: Finally, direct comparison of ATAC-seq peaks from photoreceptor and bipolar cells identified 55,402 differentially accessible regions (FDR < 0.05), 75% of which are more accessible in bipolar cells (Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Only 4263 peaks were differentially accessible between ON and OFF bipolar cells.
claims.source: While we observed significant differences in global chromatin accessibility between photoreceptors and bipolar cells, the open chromatin profiles of ON and OFF bipolar cells were largely similar, consistent with the high degree of similarity between their transcriptomes. Specifically, only 4263 peaks were differentially accessible between ON and OFF bipolar cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 79% of differential peaks between ON and OFF bipolar cells were more accessible in ON bipolar cells.
claims.source: Of note, 79% (3359) of these differential peaks were more accessible in ON bipolar cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The most highly enriched motifs within bipolar cell enhancers corresponded to CTCF, K50 HD, E-box, nuclear receptor, and MADS box motifs.
claims.source: To begin, we assessed all 319 TF binding site motifs from the HOMER database for enrichment within bipolar cell open chromatin regions (Heinz et al., 2010). The most highly enriched motifs within enhancers corresponded to CTCF, K50 HD, E-box, nuclear receptor, and MADS box motifs (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis using HOMER.

claims.claim: All of the most highly enriched motifs in bipolar cells were previously shown to be among the most enriched motifs in photoreceptor ATAC-seq peaks.
claims.source: All of these motifs were previously shown to be among the most enriched motifs in photoreceptor ATAC-seq peaks as well (Hughes et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2017.

claims.claim: K50 HD motifs were more enriched in photoreceptors than in bipolar cells.
claims.source: Although both photoreceptors and bipolar cells showed marked enrichment for K50 HD motifs, these motifs were more enriched in photoreceptors (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: E-box motifs were more enriched in bipolar cells than photoreceptors.
claims.source: Conversely, E-box motifs were more enriched in bipolar cells than photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Both monomeric and dimeric Q50 HD motifs are enriched in photoreceptor open chromatin regions but not in bipolar regions.
claims.source: The most striking difference in TF binding site enrichment between the two cell classes was the enrichment of both monomeric and dimeric Q50 HD motifs in photoreceptor open chromatin regions and their lack of enrichment in bipolar regions (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: RAX is the most well-characterized Q50 HD TF expressed in photoreceptors.
claims.source: The most well-characterized Q50 HD TF expressed in photoreceptors is RAX, which is required for cone gene expression and survival (Irie et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Irie et al., 2015.

claims.claim: RAX is required for cone gene expression and survival.
claims.source: The most well-characterized Q50 HD TF expressed in photoreceptors is RAX, which is required for cone gene expression and survival (Irie et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Irie et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Bipolar cells express multiple Q50 HD TFs (VSX2, VSX1, ISL1, LXH3, LHX4, AND SEBOX).
claims.source: In contrast, bipolar cells express multiple Q50 HD TFs (VSX2, VSX1, ISL1, LXH3, LHX4, AND SEBOX) (Shekhar et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shekhar et al., 2016.

claims.claim: VSX2 is required for bipolar cell development and is expressed in all mouse bipolar cell types throughout development and into adulthood.
claims.source: VSX2 is required for bipolar cell development and is expressed in all mouse bipolar cell types throughout development and into adulthood (Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Liu et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Livne-Bar et al., 2006; Liu et al., 1994.

claims.claim: VSX2 acts as a repressor of photoreceptor CREs.
claims.source: The paradoxical absence of Q50 HD motif enrichment in bipolar open chromatin regions despite the presence of multiple Q50 HD TFs in this cell class may be explained by the observation that VSX2 acts as a repressor of photoreceptor CREs (Dorval et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dorval et al., 2006.

claims.claim: There is a modest correlation between enhancer accessibility and gene expression.
claims.source: As described in previous studies, we observed a modest correlation between enhancer accessibility and gene expression, and a more robust correlation between promoter accessibility and gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Hughes et al., 2017; Pastor et al., 2014; Ampuja et al., 2017; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to Hughes et al., 2017; Pastor et al., 2014; Ampuja et al., 2017; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2018.

claims.claim: There is a more robust correlation between promoter accessibility and gene expression than between enhancer accessibility and gene expression.
claims.source: As described in previous studies, we observed a modest correlation between enhancer accessibility and gene expression, and a more robust correlation between promoter accessibility and gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Hughes et al., 2017; Pastor et al., 2014; Ampuja et al., 2017; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to Hughes et al., 2017; Pastor et al., 2014; Ampuja et al., 2017; de la Torre-Ubieta et al., 2018.

claims.claim: 8435 enhancer regions are accessible either in photoreceptors or bipolar cells, but not accessible in brain, liver or splenic B cells.
claims.source: We identified 8435 enhancer regions which are accessible either in photoreceptors or bipolar cells, but not accessible in brain, liver or splenic B cells (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: About 46% of the differentially accessible peaks were more open in bipolar cells.
claims.source: We found that ~ 46% (3,270) of the differentially accessible peaks were more open in bipolar cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: The photoreceptor peak set contains known enhancers responsible for driving cell type-specific expression of Rhodopsin (Rho) and components of the rod-specific phototransduction cascade.
claims.source: Indeed, the photoreceptor peak set contains known enhancers responsible for driving cell type-specific expression of Rhodopsin (Rho) and components of the rod-specific phototransduction cascade (Corbo et al., 2010; Nie et al., 1996)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Corbo et al., 2010; Nie et al., 1996.

claims.claim: The bipolar peak set contains a known enhancer that drives Vsx2 expression in bipolar cells.
claims.source: while the bipolar peak set contains a known enhancer that drives Vsx2 expression in bipolar cells (Kim et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Bipolar-selective regions were markedly enriched for E-box motifs but completely lacked enrichment for Q50 HD motifs.
claims.source: The bipolar-selective regions were markedly enriched for E-box motifs but completely lacked enrichment for Q50 HD motifs (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Photoreceptor-selective regions were enriched for Q50 HD motifs, but lacked E-box motif enrichment.
claims.source: Conversely, photoreceptor-selective regions were enriched for Q50 HD motifs, but lacked E-box motif enrichment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: CTCF enrichment was absent in all but the unfiltered peak set.
claims.source: Of note, CTCF enrichment was absent in all but the unfiltered peak set, suggesting that the CTCF enrichment observed in Figure 4 is attributable to ubiquitously accessible peaks.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Gnb3 encodes the β subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein required for cone phototransduction as well as ON bipolar cell function.
claims.source: Gnb3 encodes the β subunit of a heterotrimeric G-protein required for cone phototransduction as well as ON bipolar cell function (Dhingra et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dhingra et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Gnb3 is expressed in rods, cones, and bipolar cells during early postnatal retinal development in the mouse.
claims.source: Gnb3 is expressed in rods, cones, and bipolar cells during early postnatal retinal development in the mouse.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a known fact.

claims.claim: Selective repression of Gnb3 in rods by the nuclear receptor TF NR2E3 results in a cone + bipolar pattern after postnatal day 10.
claims.source: Selective repression of Gnb3 in rods by the nuclear receptor TF NR2E3 results in a cone + bipolar pattern after postnatal day 10 (Haider et al., 2009; Corbo and Cepko, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Haider et al., 2009; Corbo and Cepko, 2005.

claims.claim: Mutations in K50 motifs 2, 4 and 5 in the Gnb3 promoter resulted in coordinate loss of expression in both photoreceptor and bipolar cells.
claims.source: Mutations in K50 motifs 2, 4 and 5 resulted in coordinate loss of expression in both photoreceptor and bipolar cells, indicating that these motifs are required for reporter expression in both cell classes (Figure 6B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claims.claim: Mutations in K50 site 1 or 3 in the Gnb3 promoter had no effect on expression in either photoreceptors or bipolar cells.
claims.source: Conversely, mutations in site 1 or 3 had no effect on expression in either cell class (Figure 6B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claims.claim: Replacement of K50 motif site three with a Q50 motif caused a selective decrease in bipolar expression with no change in photoreceptor expression.
claims.source: Whereas introduction of a Q50 motif into site one had no apparent effect, replacement of site three caused a selective decrease in bipolar expression with no change in photoreceptor expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data.

claims.claim: Introduction of Q50 motifs into both sites 1 and 3 of the Gnb3 promoter markedly reduced reporter expression in bipolar cells, with no effect on photoreceptor expression.
claims.source: When we introduced Q50 motifs into both sites, reporter expression was markedly reduced in bipolar cells, with no effect on photoreceptor expression (Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells have divergent transcriptomes but share remarkably similar cis-regulatory grammars, marked by enrichment of K50 homeodomain binding sites.
claims.source: By comparing open chromatin maps and transcriptomic profiles, we found that while photoreceptor and bipolar cells have divergent transcriptomes, they share remarkably similar cis-regulatory grammars, marked by enrichment of K50 homeodomain binding sites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined analysis of ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cell class-specific enhancers are distinguished by enrichment of E-box motifs in bipolar cells, and Q50 homeodomain motifs in photoreceptors.
claims.source: However, cell class-specific enhancers are distinguished by enrichment of E-box motifs in bipolar cells, and Q50 homeodomain motifs in photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of cell class-specific enhancers.

claims.claim: Converting K50 motifs to Q50 motifs represses reporter expression in bipolar cells, while photoreceptor expression is maintained.
claims.source: We show that converting K50 motifs to Q50 motifs represses reporter expression in bipolar cells, while photoreceptor expression is maintained.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Partitioning of Q50 motifs within cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements was a critical step in the evolutionary divergence of the bipolar transcriptome from that of photoreceptors.
claims.source: These findings suggest that partitioning of Q50 motifs within cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements was a critical step in the evolutionary divergence of the bipolar transcriptome from that of photoreceptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cellular diversity arises in the course of evolution through a 'division of labor' process, in which a multifunctional ancestral cell type gives rise to descendant cell types with divergent and novel functions.
claims.source: It has been proposed that cellular diversity arises in the course of evolution through a 'division of labor' process, in which a multifunctional ancestral cell type gives rise to descendant cell types with divergent and novel functions (Arendt et al., 2009; Brunet and King, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arendt et al., 2009; Brunet and King, 2017.

claims.claim: The elimination of Q50 motifs from bipolar-specific CREs likely played a key role in differentiating the bipolar transcriptome from that of photoreceptors during early stages of vertebrate retinal evolution.
claims.source: We propose that the elimination of Q50 motifs from bipolar-specific CREs likely played a key role in differentiating the bipolar transcriptome from that of photoreceptors during early stages of vertebrate retinal evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: VSX2 plays a genome-wide role in silencing photoreceptor gene expression in bipolar cells.
claims.source: Our results generalize this conclusion, suggesting that VSX2 plays a genome-wide role in silencing photoreceptor gene expression in bipolar cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the motif enrichment patterns and reporter assay results.

claims.claim: VSX2 promotes V2a interneuron identity by directly repressing the motor neuron gene expression program and by competing for Q50 sites at motor neuron enhancers in the spinal cord.
claims.source: A similar role for VSX2 has recently been described in the spinal cord, where closely related progenitor cells give rise to either motor neurons or V2a interneurons (Clovis et al., 2016). VSX2 promotes V2a identity by directly repressing the motor neuron gene expression program and by competing for Q50 sites at motor neuron enhancers.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Clovis et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The transcriptomes of ON and OFF cone bipolar cells are more similar to each other than to that of rod bipolar cells.
claims.source: In a paper that appeared after our profiling studies had been performed, Shekhar et al. (2016) documented the single-cell expression profiles of individual bipolar cell types and showed that the transcriptomes of ON and OFF cone bipolar cells are more similar to each other than to that of rod bipolar cells (RBCs).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shekhar et al., 2016.

claims.claim: RBCs constitute nearly 60% of the cells in the ON bipolar population analyzed in this study.
claims.source: We estimate that RBCs constitute nearly 60% of the cells in our ON population (RBCs compose 56% of ON bipolar cells identified in Shekhar et al., 2016, and ~ 57% of those identified as ON BCs by Wässle et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is an estimate based on data from Shekhar et al., 2016 and Wässle et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In some turtle species ~ 30% of the cell bodies in the photoreceptor layer belong to bipolar cells, not photoreceptors.
claims.source: In some turtle species ~ 30% of the cell bodies in the photoreceptor layer (the outer nuclear layer) belong to bipolar cells, not photoreceptors (Tauchi, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tauchi, 1990.

claims.claim: Displaced bipolar cells possess an inner segment-like process that extends to the outer limiting membrane and contains abundant mitochondria and a sensory-type ('9 + 0') cilium.
claims.source: These so-called 'displaced bipolar cells' possess an inner segment-like process that extends to the outer limiting membrane and contains abundant mitochondria and even a sensory-type ('9 + 0') cilium (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 7A,B.

claims.claim: Bipolar cells with Landolt's club occur in nearly all non-mammalian vertebrate classes and even in some mammalian species.
claims.source: Another intermediate type of bipolar cell occurs in nearly all non-mammalian vertebrate classes and even in some mammalian species (Hendrickson, 1966; Locket, 1970; Quesada and Génis-Gálvez, 1985; Young and Vaney, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hendrickson, 1966; Locket, 1970; Quesada and Génis-Gálvez, 1985; Young and Vaney, 1990.

claims.claim: Landolt's club extends from the cell's dendritic arbor to the outer limiting membrane and contains abundant mitochondria and a sensory-type cilium.
claims.source: This bipolar type has a nucleus localized to the inner nuclear layer, but retains an inner segment-like structure (Landolt's club), which extends from the cell's dendritic arbor to the outer limiting membrane and contains abundant mitochondria and a sensory-type cilium (Figure 7A) (Hendrickson, 1966; Locket, 1970; Quesada and Génis-Gálvez, 1985).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hendrickson, 1966; Locket, 1970; Quesada and Génis-Gálvez, 1985 and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Displaced bipolar cells and those with a Landolt's club represent 'transitional forms' on the evolutionary path from photoreceptor to typical bipolar cell.
claims.source: We suggest that displaced bipolar cells and those with a Landolt's club represent 'transitional forms' on the evolutionary path from photoreceptor to typical bipolar cell.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary interpretation of the observed cell types.

claims.claim: Bipolar cells may have evolved via the stepwise repression of discrete gene modules required for the development of individual cellular features specific to photoreceptors.
claims.source: The existence of these transitional forms suggests that bipolar cells may have evolved via the stepwise repression of discrete gene modules required for the development of individual cellular features, or 'apomeres', that are specific to photoreceptors (Arendt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary model based on the existence of transitional cell types and citation to Arendt et al., 2016.

claims.claim: RAX is expressed in developing vertebrate rods and cones and is required for normal activation of photoreceptor gene expression in mice.
claims.source: The Q50 HD TF, RAX, is expressed in developing vertebrate rods and cones and is required for normal activation of photoreceptor gene expression in mice (Irie et al., 2015; Rodgers et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Irie et al., 2015; Rodgers et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The expression of a RAX homolog in the photoreceptors of the tadpole larva of the protochordate, Ciona intestinalis, suggests a primordial role for this Q50 HD TF in activating photoreceptor gene expression in chordates.

claims.claim: Both K50 and Q50 motifs were present in the CREs of the ancestral vertebrate photoreceptor prior to the evolutionary emergence of bipolar cells.
claims.source: These data suggest that both K50 and Q50 motifs were present in the CREs of the ancestral vertebrate photoreceptor prior to the evolutionary emergence of bipolar cells, and that both K50 (OTX2 and CRX) and Q50 (RAX) HD TFs were required for gene activation in that ancestral cell type (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the data and illustrated in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The emergent expression of a repressive Q50 HD TF (VSX2) in a primordial bipolar cell would have permitted selective repression of CREs containing Q50 motifs.
claims.source: In this context, the emergent expression of a repressive Q50 HD TF (VSX2) in a primordial bipolar cell would have permitted selective repression of CREs containing Q50 motifs, allowing the cis-regulatory landscape of the two nascent cell types to begin to diverge.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claims.source: These evolutionary considerations suggest that the modern vertebrate retina arose from an ancestral retina in which photoreceptors directly synapse onto projection neurons (i.e., ganglion cells) without an intervening layer of interneurons (left side of Figure 7C).

results.result: The authors successfully isolated and characterized ON and OFF bipolar cell populations from mouse retina using FACS with Otx2-GFP and Grm6-YFP transgenic mice. Purity was confirmed by RT-qPCR showing enrichment of appropriate markers, and RNA-seq generated highly reproducible profiles across biological replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 provide converging evidence for successful isolation of bipolar cell populations. The fluorescence patterns (C26, C27), RT-qPCR validation (C28), and high reproducibility of RNA-seq (C29) collectively demonstrate robust methodology. The data in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 support these claims.

results.result: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells exhibit divergent transcriptomes with 5,259 differentially expressed genes (FDR < 0.05), including 394 transcriptional regulators. Despite this divergence, bipolar cells are transcriptionally more similar to photoreceptors than to other retinal cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are well-supported by RNA-seq data analysis. The use of Nrl-/- photoreceptors as blue cone surrogates is validated by prior literature (C30). The quantification of differentially expressed genes (C31, C33) and comparison to single-cell data (C32) provide robust evidence for transcriptional divergence between these sister cell types.

results.result: ON and OFF bipolar cells show high transcriptional similarity with only 680 differentially expressed genes, less than half the number between rod and cone photoreceptors. Bulk RNA-seq correlates well with single-cell data (PCC 0.82-0.85) and identifies 50 additional genes not detected by Drop-seq.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate the similarity between ON and OFF bipolar cells through multiple lines of evidence. The comparison to photoreceptor subtypes (C35), validation against single-cell data (C36), and identification of additional genes (C37) provide comprehensive support. Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows strong correlations.

results.result: ATAC-seq analysis revealed that bipolar cells have a more accessible chromatin landscape than photoreceptors, with 55,402 differentially accessible regions (75% more open in bipolar cells). Hierarchical clustering showed that retinal cell types cluster separately from other tissues, with whole retina DNase-seq unexpectedly clustering with bipolar cells rather than photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 are well-supported by ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data. The high reproducibility (C38), comprehensive peak identification (C39), clustering patterns (C40-C41), and differential accessibility analysis (C43-C44) are all backed by data shown in Figure 3. The unexpected clustering of whole retina with bipolar cells (C41) is particularly interesting and supported by prior work (C42).

results.result: ON and OFF bipolar cells show minimal differences in chromatin accessibility with only 4,263 differentially accessible peaks, of which 79% are more accessible in ON bipolar cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by ATAC-seq analysis and consistent with the transcriptional similarity between ON and OFF bipolar cells. The quantification is clear and the asymmetry toward ON bipolar cells is notable.

results.result: Motif enrichment analysis revealed that bipolar cells and photoreceptors share enrichment for K50 HD, E-box, CTCF, nuclear receptor, and MADS box motifs. However, K50 HD motifs are more enriched in photoreceptors, E-box motifs are more enriched in bipolar cells, and Q50 HD motifs are enriched only in photoreceptors, not in bipolar cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are strongly supported by comprehensive motif enrichment analysis using HOMER. The differential enrichment patterns are clearly shown in Figure 4 and represent a key finding distinguishing the cis-regulatory grammars of these cell types. The paradoxical absence of Q50 motif enrichment in bipolar cells despite expression of Q50 TFs (C51) is particularly significant.

results.result: RAX is the primary Q50 HD TF in photoreceptors and is required for cone gene expression and survival. In contrast, bipolar cells express multiple Q50 HD TFs including VSX2, which is required for bipolar cell development and acts as a repressor of photoreceptor CREs, potentially explaining the absence of Q50 motif enrichment in bipolar open chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 synthesize prior literature to explain the observed motif enrichment patterns. The citations supporting RAX function (C52-C53), VSX2 expression and function (C54-C56), and the proposed repressive mechanism (C56) are appropriate. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the key observation in C51.

results.result: Analysis of retina-specific enhancers (8,435 regions accessible in photoreceptors or bipolar cells but not in brain, liver, or B cells) revealed that bipolar-selective regions are enriched for E-box motifs but lack Q50 HD motifs, while photoreceptor-selective regions show the opposite pattern. These regions include known enhancers for cell type-specific genes like Rho and Vsx2.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C65 describe a refined analysis focusing on retina-specific regulatory elements. The filtering strategy to exclude ubiquitously accessible regions is sound, and the differential motif enrichment patterns (C63-C64) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 5D. The inclusion of known enhancers (C61-C62) validates the approach. The observation about CTCF (C65) provides important context.

results.result: Reporter assays using the Gnb3 promoter demonstrated that K50 motifs 2, 4, and 5 are required for expression in both photoreceptors and bipolar cells, while sites 1 and 3 are dispensable. Critically, converting K50 sites to Q50 motifs (particularly at sites 1 and 3 together) selectively represses expression in bipolar cells while maintaining photoreceptor expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 provide direct experimental validation of the proposed role of Q50 motifs in repressing bipolar cell expression. The reporter assays are well-designed with appropriate controls, and the results clearly demonstrate selective repression in bipolar cells when Q50 motifs are introduced (C71-C72). The data in Figure 6 strongly support these claims. This is a key functional validation of the computational findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that photoreceptors and bipolar cells share similar cis-regulatory grammars marked by K50 HD motif enrichment, but are distinguished by differential enrichment of E-box motifs in bipolar cells and Q50 HD motifs in photoreceptors. Converting K50 to Q50 motifs represses bipolar expression while maintaining photoreceptor expression, suggesting that Q50 motif partitioning was critical for evolutionary divergence of these sister cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 represent the main conclusions of the paper. They are well-supported by the combined evidence from ATAC-seq (showing similar overall patterns but differential motif enrichment), RNA-seq (showing transcriptional divergence), and reporter assays (demonstrating functional consequences of motif changes). The evolutionary interpretation (C76) is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors propose an evolutionary model in which bipolar cells diverged from photoreceptors through elimination of Q50 motifs from bipolar-specific CREs, with VSX2 playing a genome-wide role in silencing photoreceptor gene expression in bipolar cells. This mechanism is analogous to VSX2's role in spinal cord V2a interneuron specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 present an evolutionary model based on the experimental findings. While the model is plausible and supported by the data presented in this study (C79) and analogous systems (C80), it remains speculative regarding the actual evolutionary history (C78). The model is internally consistent but would require additional comparative genomic or evolutionary studies to be fully validated.

results.result: The ON bipolar population analyzed contains approximately 60% rod bipolar cells (RBCs), and BC5D cells (2.3% of bipolar cells) were excluded from both ON and OFF populations due to low Grm6-YFP expression, as confirmed by analysis of a YFP-low population.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 and C100 address an important limitation of the study. The estimate of RBC composition (C82) is based on published single-cell data and is reasonable. The exclusion of BC5D cells (C100) is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and the authors appropriately note that this rare population's absence likely does not materially impact the analysis.

results.result: The authors describe 'transitional' bipolar cell types found in non-mammalian vertebrates that possess photoreceptor-like features (displaced bipolar cells with cell bodies in the ONL and Landolt's club structures containing cilia and mitochondria). These are proposed to represent evolutionary intermediates between photoreceptors and typical bipolar cells, suggesting evolution via stepwise repression of photoreceptor-specific gene modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 synthesize comparative anatomical observations from the literature to support the evolutionary model. The descriptions of transitional cell types (C83-C86) are well-cited, and the interpretation as evolutionary intermediates (C87-C88) is reasonable, though speculative. This provides important comparative context for the molecular findings.

results.result: The authors propose that the ancestral vertebrate photoreceptor expressed both K50 (OTX2, CRX) and Q50 (RAX) HD TFs and contained both motif types in CREs. The modern vertebrate retina likely arose from an ancestral retina where photoreceptors directly synapsed onto ganglion cells, as seen in hagfish and parietal eyes. Emergent VSX2 expression in primordial bipolar cells would have enabled selective repression of Q50-containing CREs.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C95 present a detailed evolutionary model. While the molecular components are well-supported by data from extant species (C89-C90, C94-C95), the proposed ancestral states and evolutionary transitions (C91-C93) are speculative inferences. The model is plausible and consistent with available evidence, but direct validation would require comparative genomic studies across vertebrate lineages or functional studies in basal vertebrates.

results.result: Despite rods constituting ~80% of retinal cells, whole retina DNase-seq clustered with bipolar cells rather than photoreceptors. Photoreceptor and bipolar cell ATAC-seq peaks account for 83% of whole-retina peaks, with bipolar peaks showing greater overlap with brain DNase-seq (47% vs 37%). An overall correlation exists between chromatin accessibility and gene expression, though not at all loci.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe unexpected but well-documented findings about chromatin accessibility patterns. The clustering result (C96-C97) is surprising but clearly shown in the data and explained by prior observations of global chromatin closure in rods. The tissue comparisons (C98) and correlation patterns (C99) are appropriately qualified and supported by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Photoreceptors and bipolar cells are canonical sister cell types that arise from the same OTX2-expressing progenitors, share morphological features (elongate morphology, ribbon synapses unique to these cell types), and exhibit transitional forms in some species that point to the evolutionary origin of bipolar cells from photoreceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 establish the biological context for the study through well-cited prior literature. These claims about developmental origin (C3), shared features (C4-C6), transitional cell types (C7), and evolutionary relationships (C8) are appropriately supported by multiple citations and provide essential background for interpreting the molecular findings.

results.result: CRX and OTX2 (K50 HD TFs) are master regulators in both photoreceptors and bipolar cells, while VSX2 (Q50 HD TF) is specific to bipolar cells and required for bipolar fate. K50 and Q50 homeodomains differ in their binding preferences (TAATCC vs TAATTA/G), with a single amino acid substitution toggling specificity. Various bHLH TFs also play important roles in both cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C16 summarize well-established molecular biology of transcription factor binding and function in these cell types. The claims about TF expression patterns (C9-C10), DNA binding specificity (C11-C13), and functional roles (C14-C16) are all appropriately cited and provide essential molecular context for the study.

results.result: Prior work from the authors' lab showed that photoreceptor CREs are enriched for K50 HD motifs, with K50 and E-box motifs positively correlated with enhancer activity and Q50 motifs weakly negatively correlated. Q50 motifs mediate weak activation via RAX in photoreceptors but strong repression via VSX2 in bipolar cells. Single base pair changes in HD motifs can switch cell type-specific expression in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C25 summarize relevant prior work that motivates the current study. The citations to the authors' previous work (C17-C20) and other studies (C21-C25) are appropriate and establish the foundation for investigating Q50 motif function in bipolar cells. The Drosophila example (C25) provides important precedent for the functional importance of subtle motif changes.
